ut_original_meat_wall.blurb: A varnished sandstone wall in Indian Creek, near Monticello in southeast Utah, holding about sixteen trad crack lines. Grades are split evenly between 5.10 and 5.11, which is a gentler spread than much of the canyon, so it suits climbers working up from moderate cracks. Most lines take hand and wide-hand sizes, with a few thinner ones mixed in. The wall faces south and catches plenty of sun, making it a natural pick for cold days and a poor one for midsummer afternoons. The walk-in follows a rough, washed-out road before a trail splits off toward the base.

ut_vector_madness_wall.blurb: A quiet crag in Big Cottonwood Canyon, tucked into the gully east of Geezer Wall near Stairs Gulch. Roughly sixteen routes mix trad and sport: eleven trad lines and five bolted ones, running from easy fifth class up to low 5.12, with the bulk in the 5.10 range. The wall faces northeast and stays well shaded, and it is far less visited than the walls closer to the trail. Plan on 20 to 30 minutes of uphill walking from the trail past Dead Snag, finishing with a talus and brush gully.

ut_moss_ledges.blurb: A small crag in Big Cottonwood Canyon set behind a former picnic area, with a creek and big trees that provide lots of shade. Sixteen routes, almost all trad plus a single boulder problem, run from easy to low 5.12, with most between 5.9 and 5.10. The rock is broken and steep, protection comes from a blend of bolts, pitons and cams, and many lines wander, so long slings help. Walk up the staircase at the back of the picnic area to reach the wall. Hikers heading to a waterfall pass nearby.

ut_mule_hollow_wall.blurb: A 500-foot east-facing wall in Big Cottonwood Canyon, reached by a steep walk of about 45 to 60 minutes up a gulch from the canyon road. It is mainly a multi-pitch trad destination, with six bolted routes among the sixteen. Grades span 5.5 to 5.10, with most lines in the 5.6 to 5.9 range, which makes it a fitting step up for moderate trad leaders. The remote, alpine feel and the effort of getting there keep crowds thin. Expect talus and a steep, loose final scramble to the base.

ut_adjective_the.blurb: A steep limestone fin beside the streambed in Rock Canyon, just east of Provo. All sixteen routes are bolted sport climbs, and the grades lean hard: one 5.9, a few 5.10s, then a big cluster of 5.11 and four at 5.12. Tree cover shades the east-facing wall, which makes it a comfortable choice for hot summer afternoons and evenings. From the first wooden bridge in the canyon, stay on the near side of the stream and follow the base of the cliff to its north end.

ut_temple_of_sinawava.blurb: Sandstone cliffs at the head of Zion Canyon, where the scenic road ends. Climbing here is mostly trad with a couple of aid routes, ranging from 5.8 to 5.12, with half of the sixteen climbs in the 5.10 range. Several routes are multi-pitch, and a darkly varnished corner line is the area's best-known objective. The walls are close to the road end and bus stop, so some short routes are quick to reach. The rock is fragile after rain, so let it dry fully before pulling on holds.

ut_fast_food_joint.blurb: A short sport wall right beside Maple Canyon Road in central Utah, on the north side of the road not far up-canyon from Box Canyon. It has sixteen bolted routes, and most are easy: roughly half sit between 5.5 and 5.7, with more at 5.8 and 5.9 and a couple at 5.10. That makes it one of the better places in the canyon for beginners and for warming up. Brush partly hides the wall from the road, and the walk from the car is only a few minutes. Expect company on busy weekends.

ut_suburbia.blurb: A trad crag in Indian Creek, near Moab, high above a huge talus cone and away from the busy walls near the road. Fifteen of the sixteen routes are trad, with one alpine-style line, and grades run from 5.8 to 5.12, mostly 5.10 with a handful of 5.11s. A long 5.12 splitter is the standout, and a few obvious lines were still unclimbed at last report. Newer lines have steel anchors. Approach from the parking at The Wall, crossing washes and following an old mining road up the talus, which takes real effort.
